rv.q: One of its most enjoyable shows has arrived just in time.
It’s another magnificent performance — kind-eyed, honey-voiced and all but irresistible.
Spectacular! That's the word, in my opinion, that best describes Just in Time, the endlessly show-stopping new musical.

In the end, people will come mostly to see Groff, as well they should. He’s fabulous. Plus the timing is just right as this musical-theater actor, shy all those years ago in “Spring Awakening,” now takes up the vital mantle of big Broadway star, a status he has approached before but never fully inhabited. Not until Bobby Darin came along to help.
Just in Time is a helluva good time at the theater.
Groff dazzles us with joyful firework bursts
Paradoxically, in illuminating the life of a comparatively minor star, the show’s creators have breathed fresh life into one of Broadway’s most exhausted genres.
Jonathan Groff uses his considerable charisma to embody the late singer with pizzazz in a rousing yet incomplete Broadway show

Only Lawrence, arriving on Broadway after The Sex Lives of College Girls, is able to briefly wrench the show’s center of gravity away from Groff, and only because her belt is so full it bursts through the theater like Alice expanding past the size of a house in Wonderland.
Dismayed as I was to endure so much else, I have to admit he’s giving one of Broadway’s best performances.
Although a bio-jukebox need not necessarily glorify its subject, it must at minimum justify why they are the subject of a musical in the first place, which "Just in Time" never does.

In Just in Time, a jukebox homage to Bobby Darin now at the Circle in the Square, he harnesses his multi-threat talents into a performance that is part impression, part confession, and entirely memorable.
As well she should be, since Groff is delivering a career-defining highlight that is sure to be talked about for years to come.
We are high on the story of Bobby Darin.
In Time does conclude, it goes out with an exuberant bang, and though the vapor forms, it's clear that this is a show guaranteed to linger.
The meta-theatricality of Just in Time, exemplified by Alex Timbers's direction and Jonathan Groff's performance, injects freshness into the jukebox bio-musical.
Groff could earn back-to-back Tony Awards with this tour-de-force performance.
Just in Time succeeds greatly more as an experience than a cohesive musical, with Leight and Oliver's book eventually succumbing to typical bio-musical choppiness in its second act.

Buoyed by Andrew Resnick and Michael Thurber’s kicky orchestrations, his renditions of Darin’s standards—the brassy, hard-edged “Mack the Knife,” with those insistent key changes, and the absolutely manic, horn-crazed “Once in a Lifetime”—are thrilling.

Groff’s vehicle, and he rides it splendidly, and tirelessly. I’ll admit I was never a huge fan of Darin; notwithstanding his undeniable technical prowess, his delivery could, for me, have a smarmy, lounge-lizard quality.
Groff is simply sensational in both his roles, charming as himself and astonishing in his revelatory Darin.
That, too, is something that Groff delivers in spades, determined to draw us in at least as much as the man he portrays ever did.
How rare it is for a jukebox bio-musical to feel like it comes genuinely from the heart.
Bobby Darin frankly does not strike me as having either the endurance in the culture or a uniquely compelling enough story to be the most obvious figure to build a Broadway show around.
It’s a lovely concert, but not a revelatory show about the life of Bobby Darin.
When Groff is singing and dancing (stunning choreography by Shannon Lewis), “Just in Time” absolutely dazzles.
His ability to connect with both fellow actors, such as Darin’s two major love interests, Connie Francis (Gracie Lawrence) and Sandra Dee (Erika Henningsen), and the audience alike is uncanny.

Groff is a true star, maybe in a way that Darin always dreamed of, and with his performance in Just In Time, Groff, the wettest and most wonderful man on Broadway, may well have moved up and beyond the character he is embodying in this bio musical.
It’s a slam-bang, love-struck miracle — and baby, it’s right on time.
For me, Just in Time is a moment worth holding on to.
While it's hard to resist Groff's considerable charms, he struggles to sell us on Darin'
Overall, “Just in Time” is a captivating musical from start to finish.

cn.t: Jonathan Groff dazzles as Bobby Darin in this slick, entertaining bio-musical that doesn't reinvent the jukebox genre but succeeds on star power and showmanship. Critics praise Groff's charisma and vocals, though some find the by-the-numbers format familiar.

sg.ra: In the 3/4 thrust configuration these front rows put you at the lip of the playing area with actors entering from aisles directly beside you. Headout notes rows AA-B are 'closest to the stage' and audiences are 'roped into the play's action.' Because the stage is surrounded on three sides, the acting is deliberately blocked so no front row gets a sustained back-of-actor view, but individual moments will face away from you — that is inherent to in-the-round and not a flaw of this section.

Universally cited as the optimal vantage in this thrust venue — close enough to feel the intimacy of a 776-seat room with only 10 rows, but one row back from the front so sightlines catch the whole three-sided playing area. Headout: 'Center Orchestra - rows B, C and D' positioned centrally are 'possibly the best seats in the house.' The in-the-round blocking is designed so these central rows at eye-level with the floor see choreography and staging as intended.

Because the venue only has 10 rows total and stadium-inclined seating, rows H-I still feel close to the thrust while giving elevated sightlines that reveal staging patterns on the floor — useful for musicals with choreography. Headout: 'Rows H and I in the upper middle level offer a great view of the stage and the prices are lower than those of the premium orchestra seats.' AVFMS reviewer MusicaltheatreWhiz in H144 (Just in Time, Feb 2026): 'There really isn't a bad seat in the house!' TripAdvisor: 'up is better for musicals.'

In a typical Broadway house the last row would be a skip, but Circle in the Square is only 10 rows deep so row K is roughly where Row G would be in a standard theater. AVFMS danielb9 at K109 (Just in Time, Feb 28 2026): 'Enough legroom to be comfortable and despite being in the back row felt very connected to the action.' Multiple reviews note 'no obstruction' and 'great seat' for row K. Stadium incline ensures sightlines over heads. The in-the-round nature means some scenes still play toward the opposite side, but this is a venue property not a section flaw.

sg.n: Side Sections - Long Arms of the Horseshoe (100s & 200s)
sg.ra: The two long 'wide sides' of the horseshoe (the 100 and 200 numbered sections per BWW forum user Patash's question about 102/202 numbering) give a profile view of the main action. TripAdvisor: 'the two wide sides are fine' and are preferred over 'straight in front' which is 'too far from the rear end of the main stage.' AVFMS samr32 at C207 (Just in Time, Feb 26 2026): 'Amazing seat! Can see both stages so well, and the actors (including Jonathan Groff) run up and down the aisle right near you.' The 300-degree blocking means side sections regularly get face-forward moments; not behind-stage.

The one sustained warning across every source is the extreme corner seats where the horseshoe's ends meet the stage. Headout/TickPick specifically: 'seats 438-440 are obstructed when actors perform on the far left of the stage and vice versa for the opposite side' (437-439). Unlike the rest of the house where in-the-round angles are temporary, these corner positions can have whole extended scenes played entirely out of view on the opposite corner. In a 3/4 thrust with actors using the full perimeter, this is a structural flaw of the seat, not a temporary blocking issue.

vr.q: Everything this show is greater than the sum of its parts. The choreography is great, the singing is great, the acting is great, the casting is great, the set design is great, the costumes are great, the lighting is great.
I can go on and on and on about it, but I just loved this. I would go back and see this again. It was dazzling.
Even if you don't know a thing about Bobby Darin or his music, you'll be hard-pressed to not have a good time here.
if you're in the same boat and you're not in a hurry to see Jonathan Groff on stage again I don't know that you need to rush to see this
